claim: Patterns of spatial positioning of individuals within microbial communities are often critical to community function.
source: Patterns of spatial positioning of individuals within microbial communities are often critical to community function.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that sets up the importance of the research topic.

claim: Understanding patterning in natural communities is hampered by the multitude of cell–cell and cell–environment interactions as well as environmental variability.
source: However, understanding patterning in natural communities is hampered by the multitude of cell–cell and cell–environment interactions as well as environmental variability.
evidence: This statement reflects established challenges in the field based on general scientific understanding.

claim: In strong cooperation with spatially localized large fitness benefits to both partners, a unique pattern is generated where partners spatially intermixed by appearing successively on top of each other.
source: We found that in strong cooperation with spatially localized large fitness benefits to both partners, a unique pattern is generated: partners spatially intermixed by appearing successively on top of each other, insensitive to initial conditions and interaction dynamics.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by both simulations and experiments described throughout the manuscript.

claim: Partner intermixing in strong cooperation is insensitive to initial conditions and interaction dynamics.
source: We found that in strong cooperation with spatially localized large fitness benefits to both partners, a unique pattern is generated: partners spatially intermixed by appearing successively on top of each other, insensitive to initial conditions and interaction dynamics.
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A, Figure 3A, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Intermixing was experimentally observed in an engineered yeast community cooperating through metabolite-exchanges.
source: Intermixing was experimentally observed in two obligatory cooperative systems: an engineered yeast community cooperating through metabolite-exchanges and a methane-producing community cooperating through redox-coupling.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F and related figures.

claim: Intermixing was experimentally observed in a methane-producing community cooperating through redox-coupling.
source: Intermixing was experimentally observed in two obligatory cooperative systems: an engineered yeast community cooperating through metabolite-exchanges and a methane-producing community cooperating through redox-coupling.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In simulated communities consisting of several species, most of the strongly-cooperating pairs appeared intermixed.
source: Even in simulated communities consisting of several species, most of the strongly-cooperating pairs appeared intermixed.
evidence: This is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 5D indicating 26 out of 31 cooperative pairs intermixed.

claim: When ecological interactions are the major patterning force, strong cooperation leads to partner intermixing.
source: Thus, when ecological interactions are the major patterning force, strong cooperation leads to partner intermixing.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by both simulations and experiments throughout the manuscript.

claim: Biological interactions drive pattern formation at different levels of organization.
source: Biological interactions drive pattern formation at different levels of organization (Murray, 2003), ranging from developmental patterning within multicellular organisms and biofilms (Shapiro, 1998; Lewis, 2008; Vlamakis et al., 2008; Chuong and Richardson, 2009), to ecological patterning within multi-species communities (Levin, 1992; Rietkerk and van de Koppel, 2008; Momeni et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: In a synthetic community, three bacterial species can only grow when they are separated by an intermediate distance.
source: Consider microbial communities: in a synthetic community, three bacterial species, each contributing an essential benefit while simultaneously competing for these benefits, can only grow when they are separated by an intermediate distance (Kim et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kim et al., 2008.

claim: Different types of patterning are correlated with different levels of biofilm growth.
source: different types of patterning are correlated with different levels of biofilm growth (Christensen et al., 2002; Brenner and Arnold, 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Christensen et al., 2002 and Brenner and Arnold, 2011.

claim: Branching colony morphology allows more effective spreading across a nutrient-poor surface.
source: branching colony morphology allows more effective spreading across a nutrient-poor surface (Levine and Ben-Jacob, 2004)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Levine and Ben-Jacob, 2004.

claim: In waste treatment granules, the layered pattern of bacteria and archaea is thought to facilitate the sequential degradation of substrates.
source: and in waste treatment granules, the layered pattern of bacteria and archaea is thought to facilitate the sequential degradation of substrates (Satoh et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Satoh et al., 2007 and includes speculative language ('is thought to').

claim: It is unclear how cell–cell and cell–environment interactions govern the patterning of communities.
source: Despite the wide-ranging importance of microbial communities in, for example, human health and the biogeochemical cycling of elements, it is still unclear how cell–cell and cell–environment interactions govern the patterning of communities (Elias and Banin, 2012).
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap in the field, supported by a citation.

claim: Understanding the mechanistic basis of pattern formation from observations of natural communities is stymied by the multitude of cell–cell and cell–environment interactions, as well as environmental variations within and across communities.
source: Understanding the mechanistic basis of pattern formation from observations of natural communities is stymied by the multitude of cell–cell and cell–environment interactions, as well as environmental variations within and across communities.
evidence: This statement reflects a general understanding of challenges in studying natural communities.

claim: It is not uncommon to observe qualitatively different patterns in samples of essentially the same type of community.
source: Thus, it is not uncommon to observe qualitatively different patterns in samples of essentially the same type of community (Christensen et al., 2002; Wilmes et al., 2008; Dekas et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Strong cooperation is important in a wide variety of microbial communities ranging from syntrophic systems critical for nutrient cycling to pathogenic biofilms.
source: This is because 1) it is important in a wide variety of microbial communities ranging from syntrophic systems critical for nutrient cycling (Schink, 2002; Falkowski et al., 2008; McInerney et al., 2009) to pathogenic biofilms (Kelly, 1980; Kolenbrander et al., 2010; Elias and Banin, 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The codependence between cooperative partners poses special challenges for isolating and culturing cells.
source: and 2) the codependence between cooperative partners poses special challenges for isolating and culturing cells (Schink, 2002; McInerney et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Schink, 2002 and McInerney et al., 2009.

claim: Interactions benefiting at least one partner could potentially allow initially disparate partner ratios to converge over time.
source: Starting with a generalized model based on fitness effects of ecological interactions between two populations (A and B) occurring at a local scale ('fitness model'), we predicted: 1) interactions benefiting at least one partner could potentially allow initially disparate partner ratios to converge over time
evidence: This prediction is supported by simulations shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Unlike other types of ecological interactions that caused partner segregation or layering, strongly cooperating partners intermixed by forming patches that successively accumulated on top of each other.
source: and 2) unlike other types of ecological interactions that caused partner segregation or layering of one population over the other (A over B or B over A), strongly cooperating partners intermixed by forming patches that successively accumulated on top of each other (A over B over A over B, etc).
evidence: This prediction is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 1C-H.

claim: Yeast cells initially divide and push other cells to the side such that all cells remain in the same plane.
source: Starting from one budding cell (a, hour 0.5), cells initially divided and pushed other cells to the side such that all cells remained in the same plane (b, hour 9).
evidence: This observation is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and Video 1.

claim: When a yeast cell group reaches approximately 5-cell radius, cells in the center can no longer push other cells to the side and instead bud upward.
source: When the group of cells reached approximately 5-cell radius (c, hour 14), cells in the center could no longer push other cells to the side and instead budded upward, as indicated by higher intensities in the fluorescence images.
evidence: This observation is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and Video 1.

claim: Continued growth of yeast microcolony forces more cells in the middle to send their progeny to upper layers, while cells close to the edge can still push other cells to the side and remain on the agarose surface.
source: Continued growth of microcolony forced more cells in the middle to send their progeny to upper layers, while cells close to the edge could still push other cells to the side and remained on the agarose surface (d, hour 17.5).
evidence: This observation is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and Video 1.

claim: For cooperation ([↑ ↑]), commensalism ([∼ ↑]), and exploitation ([↓ ↑]), different initial partner ratios can potentially converge over time.
source: Simulations (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Figure 1—source data 1) and analytical calculations ('Requirements for steady-state ratios in the six types of communities' in 'Materials and methods') show that for interactions benefiting at least one partner, including cooperation ([↑ ↑]), commensalism ([∼ ↑]), and exploitation ([↓ ↑]), different initial partner ratios can potentially converge over time (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by both simulation data and analytical calculations.

claim: Ratio convergence requires 'balanced' fitness where one partner is not always fitter than the other.
source: Ratio convergence requires 'balanced' fitness. For example, for A[∼ ↑]B to achieve ratio convergence, the basal fitness of A must be higher than that of B and after gaining the fitness benefit from commensalism, B must be able to grow at least as fast as A. This way, a situation incompatible to ratio convergence, that is, one partner always fitter than the other, does not occur.
evidence: This is an inference from the analytical model about the conditions required for ratio convergence.

claim: Population ratios converged in commensal and cooperative but not competitive yeast communities.
source: Using engineered competitive, obligatory commensal, and obligatory cooperative yeast communities (see below), we confirmed that population ratios converged in the commensal and cooperative but not competitive communities (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Convergence of population ratios reflects a balance between supply and consumption when growth is limited by supply.
source: This convergence of population ratios reflects a balance between supply and consumption when growth is limited by supply (Shou et al., 2007): if, for instance, the supplier population suddenly increased in relative abundance, then each individual in the consumer population would receive more benefit and grow faster, which would return the ratio to its original value.
evidence: This explanation is based on inference from the data and is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In [∼ ∼], [∼ ↓], and [↓ ↓], red and green populations primarily formed columns that are spatially segregated from each other.
source: In [∼ ∼], [∼ ↓], and [↓ ↓], red and green populations primarily formed columns that are spatially segregated from each other (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: This is a finding from simulations shown in Figure 1C-E.

claim: In [↑ ↓] and [∼ ↑], frequently one of the populations either formed a column or became covered by the partner population.
source: In [↑ ↓] and [∼ ↑], frequently one of the populations (green) either formed a column or became covered by the partner population (red) (Figure 1F–G).
evidence: This is a finding from simulations shown in Figure 1F-G.

claim: Only in cooperation ([↑ ↑]) conferring large fitness benefits to both partners, the two partner populations appeared to be extensively 'intermixed'.
source: Only in cooperation ([↑ ↑]) conferring large fitness benefits to both partners, the two partner populations appeared to be extensively 'intermixed', manifested as the two different cell types successively piling on top of each other (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is a finding from simulations shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Statistically significant differences in intermixing indexes were observed between strong cooperation versus other types of interactions.
source: Statistically significant differences were observed between strong cooperation versus other types of interactions (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from simulation data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Partner intermixing distinguishes strong cooperation from other ecological interactions.
source: Thus, we predicted that partner intermixing would distinguish strong cooperation from other ecological interactions.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the simulation results shown in Figure 1.

claim: Equal-fitness competitive yeast communities showed population segregation as suggested by static late-stage top-views.
source: Competitive communities of strains with equal fitness (equal-fitness competition, abbreviated as 'Eq-fitness Comp.') showed population segregation as suggested by static late-stage top-views (A, left) and columnar cross-section patterns (D, left).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 2A (left) and 2D (left).

claim: In unequal-fitness competitive communities, the fitter population expanded during growth.
source: When competing strains had different fitnesses (unequal-fitness competition, abbreviated as 'Uneq-fitness Comp.'), the fitter population G expanded during growth, as evident in top views (A, right) and vertical cross-sections (D, right).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 2A (right) and 2D (right).

claim: In obligatory commensal communities, consumers eventually overgrew and covered suppliers.
source: In obligatory commensal communities, since one supplier could support the birth of multiple consumers, consumers eventually overgrew and covered suppliers (top-views in B and vertical cross-sections in E).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 2B and 2E.

claim: Obligatory cooperative yeast communities showed substantial population intermixing as suggested by alternating cell types in top-views and patchy cross-section patterns.
source: Obligatory cooperative communities showed substantial population intermixing as suggested by alternating cell types in top-views (C, 6× magnification insets in experiments) and patchy cross-section patterns (F).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 2C and 2F.

claim: The intermixing index remained low for commensal and competitive communities.
source: Quantification of intermixing in experimental (symbols) and diffusion-model (lines) communities showed that while the intermixing index remained low for commensal (brown) and competitive (grey and black) communities, it increased linearly with community height in obligatory cooperative (magenta) communities.
evidence: This is a finding from both experiments and simulations shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The intermixing index increased linearly with community height in obligatory cooperative communities.
source: Quantification of intermixing in experimental (symbols) and diffusion-model (lines) communities showed that while the intermixing index remained low for commensal (brown) and competitive (grey and black) communities, it increased linearly with community height in obligatory cooperative (magenta) communities.
evidence: This is a finding from both experiments and simulations shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Results from the diffusion model underestimated intermixing indexes because a confined cell was modeled to divide strictly vertically upward without allowing cell movements in horizontal directions.
source: Results from the diffusion model underestimated intermixing indexes because a confined cell was modeled to divide strictly vertically upward (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) without allowing cell movements in horizontal directions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is an inference about model limitations based on comparison of model and experimental results.

claim: Local deviations from the steady-state ratio result from asymmetric partner properties and/or stochastic fluctuations in cell numbers.
source: A conceptual model illustrates the development of intermixing over time in a strongly cooperative community with 1:1 steady-state population ratio. Local deviations from the steady-state ratio result from asymmetric partner properties and/or stochastic fluctuations in cell numbers (i).
evidence: This is part of a conceptual model explaining the mechanism of intermixing shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The under-abundant population grows faster than its neighboring over-abundant partner in cooperative communities.
source: The under-abundant population (red) grows faster than its neighboring over-abundant partner (green).
evidence: This is part of a conceptual model explaining the mechanism of intermixing shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Due to the spatial localization of large cooperative benefits, cells near population borders grow faster than those farther away.
source: Due to the spatial localization of large cooperative benefits, cells near population borders grow faster than those farther away.
evidence: This is part of a conceptual model explaining the mechanism of intermixing shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Cells from the initially under-abundant population at the border divide the fastest.
source: Consequently, cells from the initially under-abundant red population at the border divide the fastest.
evidence: This is part of a conceptual model explaining the mechanism of intermixing shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Progeny that pile on the partner have more access to cooperative benefits than those who do not, which favors intermixing.
source: Progeny that pile on the green partner have more access to cooperative benefits than those who do not (ii), which favors intermixing.
evidence: This is part of a conceptual model explaining the mechanism of intermixing shown in Figure 2H.

claim: When both released nutrients were instantly and uniformly distributed throughout a community, intermixing was diminished compared to when nutrients diffused in the community.
source: The diffusion model shows that when both released nutrients were instantly and uniformly distributed throughout a community ('Coop. Instant Distr.'), intermixing was diminished compared to when nutrients diffused in the community (360 µm2/s, 'Coop.').
evidence: This is a finding from simulations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Excessive release of nutrients significantly reduced population intermixing.
source: Excessive release of nutrients (200× compared to typical values in Figure 2—source data 1) also significantly reduced population intermixing ('Coop. Excessive Release'), since the benefits exceeded the uptake capacity of partner cells and therefore no longer remained localized.
evidence: This is a finding from simulations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: If cooperative benefits were not spatially localized because of instant distribution of benefits throughout the community or because of excessive supply levels, intermixing was diminished.
source: Using the diffusion model, we found that if cooperative benefits were not spatially localized because of instant distribution of benefits throughout the community or because of excessive supply levels, intermixing was diminished (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from simulations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Local deviations from the steady-state ratio coupled with localized large cooperative benefits cause partners to 'take turns' to grow, which leads to population intermixing.
source: Based on this result and based on patterns observed in top-views and vertical cross-sections of cooperative communities, we propose that local deviations from the steady-state ratio coupled with localized large cooperative benefits cause partners to 'take turns' to grow, which leads to population intermixing (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on simulation and experimental observations.

claim: In communities engaging in strong cooperation, the intermixing index increases proportionally as a function of community height.
source: In summary, in communities engaging in strong cooperation, but not in communities governed by other types of ecological interactions, the intermixing index increases proportionally as a function of community height.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion supported by data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The proportionality of intermixing index to community height is due to a fixed patch size determined by localized nutrient supply and consumption.
source: This proportionality is due to a fixed patch size determined by localized nutrient supply and consumption.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed linear relationship and the mechanism of cooperation.

claim: The initial partner ratio did not significantly affect the level of intermixing in obligatory cooperative yeast communities.
source: We found that intermixing was insensitive to initial conditions in the yeast obligatory cooperative communities. The initial partner ratio did not significantly affect the level of intermixing (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: At very high initial cell densities, significant intermixing was observed in communities directly above the inoculation area even in the absence of cooperation.
source: At very high initial cell densities, we observed significant intermixing in communities directly above the inoculation area even in the absence of cooperation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E, yellow shading).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: High cell densities put different cell types in close proximity to one another, and cell divisions that were not perfectly straight upward caused intermixing.
source: This is because high cell densities put different cell types in close proximity to one another, and cell divisions that were not perfectly straight upward (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F) caused intermixing.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental observations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Communities beyond the inoculation area might reveal patterns indicative of the underlying interactions.
source: However, we reasoned that communities beyond the inoculation area might reveal patterns indicative of the underlying interactions, because these regions are formed by cell growth under the fitness influences of interactions.
evidence: This is a reasoning about experimental design to distinguish true cooperative intermixing from density-induced intermixing.

claim: Even though communities directly above the inoculum always appeared highly intermixed, in edge sections, significant intermixing was only observed in cooperative communities.
source: Even though communities directly above the inoculum always appeared highly intermixed (Figure 3A, 'Center' and Figure 2—figure supplement 4C), in edge sections, significant intermixing was only observed in cooperative communities (Figure 3A, 'Edge' and Figure 2—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In facultative cooperation conferring smaller fitness benefits, greater community heights are required to exhibit a significant level of intermixing.
source: In simulations using the fitness model, facultative cooperation conferring smaller fitness benefits required greater community heights to exhibit a significant level of intermixing.
evidence: This is a finding from simulations shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Partner intermixing is insensitive to diffusion constants ranging from 20 to 360 µm2/s.
source: In the diffusion model, obligatory cooperative communities with diffusion constants ranging from 20 to 360 µm2/s (corresponding to the diffusion constants of Sulforhodamine 101 in yeast community and agarose, respectively) both showed significant partner intermixing during growth.
evidence: This is a finding from simulations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Partner intermixing is insensitive to the kinetics of interactions.
source: With or without incorporating details such as significantly better starvation tolerance in adenine-requiring cells compared to lysine-requiring cells and the consequent delay in lysine release compared to adenine release (Shou et al., 2007), the diffusion model (lines) yielded substantial population intermixing.
evidence: This is a finding from simulations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Intermixing does not depend on asymmetry between cooperating partners.
source: We examined symmetric obligatory cooperation by assuming that for the two partners, all live cells released nutrients at a constant and identical rate without delay, and that other properties such as rates of growth, death, and nutrient consumption were also identical. Partner intermixing in this symmetric obligatory cooperative system (Sym. coop) was similar to that in asymmetric obligatory yeast cooperative system (Coop).
evidence: This is a finding from simulations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Intermixing relies on spatial localization of cooperative benefits that are sufficiently large to both partners, and is otherwise insensitive to initial conditions or the detailed kinetics of interactions.
source: Together, these results suggest that intermixing relies on spatial localization of cooperative benefits that are sufficiently large to both partners, and is otherwise insensitive to initial conditions or the detailed kinetics of interactions.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple simulation and experimental results.

claim: In the absence of sulfate and hydrogen, D. vulgaris and M. maripaludis engage in obligatory mutualism.
source: In the absence of sulfate and hydrogen, the two species engage in obligatory mutualism: D. vulgaris ferments lactate and promotes the growth of M. maripaludis by supplying the electron donor H2, while M. maripaludis promotes the growth of D. vulgaris by consuming the H2 gas which can be inhibitory to D. vulgaris under these conditions (Figure 4A).
evidence: This describes the cooperative interaction between the two species.

claim: D. vulgaris ferments lactate and promotes the growth of M. maripaludis by supplying the electron donor H2.
source: D. vulgaris ferments lactate and promotes the growth of M. maripaludis by supplying the electron donor H2
evidence: This describes one aspect of the cooperative interaction shown in Figure 4A.

claim: M. maripaludis promotes the growth of D. vulgaris by consuming the H2 gas which can be inhibitory to D. vulgaris under these conditions.
source: while M. maripaludis promotes the growth of D. vulgaris by consuming the H2 gas which can be inhibitory to D. vulgaris under these conditions
evidence: This describes one aspect of the cooperative interaction shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Similar types of syntrophic interactions leading to methane production typically occur in microbial consortia that digest organic compounds in freshwater sediments, sewage treatment plants, and the guts of ruminants.
source: Similar types of syntrophic interactions leading to methane production typically occur in microbial consortia that digest organic compounds in freshwater sediments, sewage treatment plants, and the guts of ruminants (Conrad et al., 1985; Schink, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Conrad et al., 1985 and Schink, 1997.

claim: Vertical cross-sections of independent D. vulgaris–M. maripaludis biofilms exhibited increasing intermixing as a function of community height.
source: Vertical cross-sections of independent D. vulgaris–M. maripaludis biofilms indeed exhibited increasing intermixing as a function of community height (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Naturally mutualistic microbes cooperating through a coupling mechanism different from metabolite exchange also exhibited a significant level of intermixing.
source: Thus, naturally mutualistic microbes cooperating through a coupling mechanism different from metabolite exchange also exhibited a significant level of intermixing.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data from D. vulgaris–M. maripaludis biofilms.

claim: Other known cooperative communities, including those degrading herbicide pollutants and those colonizing teeth, seemed to display intermixed patterns.
source: Other known cooperative communities, including those degrading herbicide pollutants (Breugelmans et al., 2008) and those colonizing teeth (Palmer et al., 2001) also seemed to display intermixed patterns, although we do not know whether the intermixing indexes of these communities increased linearly with height.
evidence: This claim is based on observations from cited literature, with a caveat about the specific pattern.

claim: In communities with more than two species, indirect interactions can obscure direct interactions.
source: In communities with more than two species, indirect interactions can obscure direct interactions (Wootton, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wootton, 2002.

claim: If A promotes B which inhibits C, it will appear that A inhibits C.
source: For example, if A promotes B which inhibits C, it will appear that A inhibits C.
evidence: This is an example illustrating how indirect interactions can obscure direct interactions.

claim: In most cases (26 out of 31), cooperative pairs intermixed in simulated five-species communities.
source: A total of 240 pair-wise interactions in 24 independent communities were examined in the fitness model. In most cases (26 out of 31), cooperative pairs intermixed (Figure 5A,D).
evidence: This is a finding from simulations shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Occasionally, commensal pairs showed substantial intermixing (3 out of 58 commensal pairs).
source: Occasionally, commensal pairs (Figure 5B, ② [∼ ↑] ③) showed substantial intermixing (3 out of 58 commensal pairs, Figure 5D)
evidence: This is a finding from simulations shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Occasionally, cooperative pairs showed little intermixing (5 out of 31).
source: or cooperative pairs (e.g., Figure 5C, ① [↑ ↑] ③) showed little intermixing (5 out of 31, Figure 5D)
evidence: This is a finding from simulations shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Deviations from expected intermixing patterns are presumably due to interactions through other community members.
source: presumably due to interactions through other community members (Figure 5B, ③ indirectly promoted ② through ④; Figure 5C, ③ promoted ⑤ which inhibited ①).
evidence: This is an inference about why some pairs deviate from expected patterns.

claim: The intermixing index reflects the 'overall' interaction between two partners, integrating any additional fitness effects of indirect interactions through other community members.
source: These deviations are consistent with the notion that the intermixing index reflects the 'overall' interaction between two partners, integrating any additional fitness effects of indirect interactions through other community members.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed deviations in multi-species communities.

claim: Strongly cooperating partners intermix while deviations from this expectation reflect the presence of strong indirect interactions.
source: Thus, strongly cooperating partners intermix while deviations from this expectation reflect the presence of strong indirect interactions.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the multi-species simulation results.

claim: Interactions conferring large fitness benefits to at least one partner ([↑ ↑], [∼ ↑], and [↓ ↑]) can potentially result in ratio convergence.
source: The first expectation is that interactions conferring large fitness benefits to at least one partner ([↑ ↑], [∼ ↑], and [↓ ↑]) can potentially result in ratio convergence (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from both simulations and experiments.

claim: In [↑ ↑] and [∼ ↑], global stability can be achieved whereas in [↓ ↑], local stability can be achieved.
source: An analytical calculation based on the fitness model showed that in [↑ ↑] and [∼ ↑], global stability can be achieved whereas in [↓ ↑], local stability can be achieved (Figure 1—figure supplement 2; 'Requirements for steady-state ratios in the six types of communities' in 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is a finding from analytical calculations.

claim: Obligatory cooperation and obligatory commensalism led disparate initial ratios to converge experimentally.
source: Experimentally, obligatory cooperation and obligatory commensalism led disparate initial ratios to converge (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: In competition between two populations of equal fitness, population ratio is determined by the initial value until a perturbation resets the value.
source: In contrast, in competition between two populations of equal fitness, population ratio is determined by the initial value until a perturbation resets the value which will remain unchanged until the next perturbation.
evidence: This is an inference about the dynamics of equal-fitness competition.

claim: In competition between two populations of unequal fitness, the fitter population should increase in frequency and therefore, population ratio is unstable.
source: In competition between two populations of unequal fitness, the fitter population should increase in frequency and therefore, population ratio is unstable.
evidence: This is an inference about the dynamics of unequal-fitness competition.

claim: In amensalism and mutual antagonism, population ratios at best have an unstable fixed point.
source: In amensalism and mutual antagonism, population ratios at best have an unstable fixed point (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a finding from analytical calculations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Strong cooperation results in partner intermixing in the direction vertical to the surface of initial colonization.
source: The second expectation is that strong cooperation results in partner intermixing in the direction vertical to the surface of initial colonization.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from the study.

claim: Cooperative intermixing requires spatially localized benefits that are sufficiently large to both partners.
source: Cooperative intermixing requires spatially localized benefits that are sufficiently large to both partners (Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and Figure 3B)
evidence: This is a conclusion based on simulation results.

claim: Cooperative intermixing appears to be robust against variations in initial conditions or reaction dynamics.
source: and otherwise appears to be robust against variations in initial conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A, Figure 3A, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D) or reaction dynamics (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple simulation and experimental results.

claim: Cooperative intermixing has been observed in the fitness model simulating strong facultative cooperation.
source: We have observed cooperative intermixing in the fitness model simulating strong facultative cooperation (Figure 1)
evidence: This is a finding from simulations shown in Figure 1.

claim: Cooperative intermixing has been observed in obligatory experimental systems including engineered yeast communities.
source: and in obligatory experimental systems including engineered yeast communities (Figure 2)
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 2.

claim: Cooperative intermixing has been observed in syntrophic methanogenic biofilms.
source: and syntrophic biofilms (Figure 4).
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 4.

claim: The intermixing indexes in cooperative communities increased linearly as a function of community height because these communities exhibited fixed-size patches associated with the spatial localization of benefits.
source: The intermixing indexes in these communities increased linearly as a function of community height, because these communities exhibited fixed-size patches associated with the spatial localization of benefits (Figure 2—figure supplement 3; 'Calculating the characteristic patch size in cooperative yeast communities' in 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental and simulation data.

claim: Other ecological interactions lead to segregated or layered patterns in which the intermixing index remained low or increased transiently before leveling off.
source: This is in stark contrast with other ecological interactions which lead to segregated or layered patterns (Figures 1 and 2) in which the intermixing index remained low or increased transiently before leveling off.
evidence: This is a finding from both simulations and experiments shown in Figures 1 and 2.
